extracted.intended_audience: hospital coders, clinical documentation specialists, health system billing staff, clinicians, and stakeholders commenting on IPPS/LTCH PPS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for assigning severity level designations (MCC, CC, NonCC) to ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes for the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS) and Long-Term Care Hospital (LTCH) PPS, including methods for review, proposed changes, and exclusions logic used in CMS rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of substantial complication or comorbidity (CC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantial complication or comorbidity was defined as a condition that, because of its presence with a specific principal diagnosis, would cause an increase in the length-of-stay by at least 1 day in at least 75 percent of the patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical physician-panel definition used to develop CC list; some diagnoses on the basic list may be excluded depending on the principal diagnosis if they are closely related. See FY 2008 IPPS final rule for original discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative categorization approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The categorization of diagnoses as an MCC, a CC, or a NonCC was accomplished using an iterative approach in which each diagnosis was evaluated to determine the extent to which its presence as a secondary diagnosis resulted in increased hospital resource use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive analysis completed for FY2008; since then CMS evaluates codes individually for new codes or requests to change severity. The iterative approach uses claims-based mathematical analyses together with clinical judgement/guiding principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical analysis of claims data (impact on resource use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mathematical analysis of claims data (Impact on Resource Use Files generated from MedPAR) to measure the impact on resource use when a diagnosis code is reported as a secondary diagnosis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS uses MedPAR files (e.g., FY2018, FY2019–FY2025 updates) and posts Impact on Resource Use Files on its website. Analyses produce C1/C2/C3 statistics used together with clinical principles. CMS hosted listening sessions and provided supplementary files for public review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Represents end of life/near death or advanced systemic physiologic decompensation and debility
rubrics_metrics.description: Represents end of life/near death or has reached an advanced stage associated with systemic physiologic decompensation and debility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of nine guiding principles applied alongside claims analysis to assess whether a secondary diagnosis indicates clinically meaningful severity that increases resource use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Denotes organ system instability or failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Denotes organ system instability or failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify diagnoses that typically require greater resources or higher levels of care when present as secondary conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Involves chronic illness with susceptibility to exacerbations or abrupt decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Involves a chronic illness with susceptibility to exacerbations or abrupt decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers whether chronic conditions have potential acute manifestations that increase resource use; CMS previously removed chronic diseases without significant acute manifestation from CC list and recognizes acute manifestations separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Serves as a marker for advanced disease states across multiple comorbid conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Serves as a marker for advanced disease states across multiple different comorbid conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis codes that indicate systemic advanced disease across comorbidities support CC/MCC designation under this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Reflects systemic impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflects systemic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions indicating systemic physiologic effects that increase complexity or resource consumption are considered under this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Post-operative/post-procedure condition/complication impacting recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-operative/post-procedure condition/complication impacting recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-procedure complications that materially affect recovery (and thus resource use) are candidates for CC/MCC designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Typically requires a higher level of care
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically requires higher level of care (that is, intensive monitoring, greater number of caregivers, additional testing, intensive care unit care, extended length of stay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify diagnoses whose presence as a secondary condition drives increased utilization (ICU, more staff, extra testing, prolonged stay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Impedes patient cooperation or management of care
rubrics_metrics.description: Impedes patient cooperation or management of care or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions that make care coordination or patient participation difficult and thereby increase resource needs are considered more severe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: Recent change in best practice or guidelines affecting expected resource use
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent (last 10 years) change in best practice, or in practice guidelines and review of the extent to which these changes have led to concomitant changes in expected resource use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS considers whether contemporary practice changes have altered expected resource consumption for a condition when assigning severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of C1/C2/C3 impact-on-resource-use statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: C1, C2, and C3 findings from the mathematical analysis indicate relative impact: a C1 value close to 2.0 suggests a condition is more like a CC than a NonCC but not as significant as an MCC; C2 values close to 3.0 suggest the condition is more similar to an MCC than a CC or NonCC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS weighs C1/C2/C3 results together (and looks for consistency) and considers low volume of cases and mixed data as important caveats. Decisions may be withheld if data are mixed or insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy principle for social determinants (SDOH Z codes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of the contribution that patient social and economic circumstances (e.g., homelessness, inadequate housing, housing instability) add to the complexity of acute hospital care should be accomplished by separately coding those diagnoses that describe an acute exacerbation or deterioration of an underlying medical condition or illness, rather than by classifying social circumstances themselves as CCs/MCCs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS aligns approach for SDOH Z codes with prior approach for chronic illnesses: severity designations should reflect clinical complexity and expected resource consumption for treating an underlying medical condition/illness, not social circumstances alone. Mathematical claims analysis is still included but contextualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of 'unspecified' diagnosis codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration to change severity level designation of 'unspecified' ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes to NonCC where there are other codes available in that code subcategory that further specify the anatomic site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS requested comment and ultimately for FY2022 maintained existing severity designations for unspecified codes but implemented a new MCE edit to provide education time; continues to consider unspecified-code policy in comprehensive reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors considered for new diagnosis codes' severity designation
rubrics_metrics.description: For new diagnosis codes, CMS first reviews the predecessor code designation, followed by review and consideration of other relevant factors including severity of illness, treatment difficulty, complexity of service and the resources utilized in the diagnosis or treatment of the condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predecessor code designation does not automatically determine new code designation; CMS may assign differently after analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: CC Exclusions List — reasons for creation
rubrics_metrics.description: The CC Exclusions List was created to: (1) preclude coding of CCs for closely related conditions; (2) preclude duplicative or inconsistent coding from being treated as CCs; and (3) ensure that cases are appropriately classified between the complicated and uncomplicated DRGs in a pair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusions modify grouper logic so certain secondary diagnoses on the CC list are not considered valid CCs in combination with particular principal diagnoses; creation was a major project involving hundreds of codes and continues to be reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: CC Exclusion principle: chronic vs acute manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronic and acute manifestations of the same condition should not be considered CCs for one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents double-counting severity where the acute manifestation is the relevant driver of resource use.

rubrics_metrics.name: CC Exclusion principle: specific vs nonspecific (NOS) codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific and nonspecific (that is, not otherwise specified (NOS)) diagnosis codes for the same condition should not be considered CCs for one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids treating overlapping specific/NOS codes as separate CC contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: CC Exclusion principle: mutually exclusive/coexisting codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes for the same condition that cannot coexist, such as partial/total, unilateral/bilateral, obstructed/unobstructed, and benign/malignant, should not be considered CCs for one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precludes logically inconsistent pairings from inflating CC count.

rubrics_metrics.name: CC Exclusion principle: anatomically proximal sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes for the same condition in anatomically proximal sites should not be considered CCs for one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents anatomically overlapping codes from being treated as separate CCs.

rubrics_metrics.name: CC Exclusion principle: closely related conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Closely related conditions should not be considered CCs for one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces inappropriate CC attribution for conditions that are clinically linked and would otherwise double-count severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and parts of the ICD-10 MS-DRGs CC Exclusion List
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICD-10 MS-DRGs CC Exclusion List (Appendix C) includes three parts: Part 1 is the list of all diagnosis codes defined as a CC or MCC when reported as a secondary diagnosis with links to principal diagnoses that would cause the CC/MCC to be considered a NonCC; Part 2 lists diagnosis codes designated as an MCC only for patients discharged alive otherwise assigned as NonCC; Part 3 lists diagnosis codes that are designated as a CC or MCC and included in the logic for listed MS-DRGs (suppression logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS proposes additions/deletions to Parts 1–3 with specific tables (6G.1, 6G.2, 6H.1, 6H.2) showing secondary/principal diagnosis order changes; tables available on CMS website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of public comment, listening sessions, and transparency in methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS solicits public comments, hosts listening sessions, provides supplemental files (mathematical data and transcripts), and considers stakeholder feedback when evaluating proposed severity level changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS paused widespread changes in prior rulemaking to provide additional background on methodology and clinical rationale; stakeholder input has influenced postponement, further analysis, and refinement of proposals (examples include FY2020–FY2025 rulemaking history).
